title: Treat Your Leader as a Coach
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This brief Admired Leadership piece addresses team members rather than leaders, arguing that the people most eager to learn often ignore the best source of learning available to them: their own boss. It observes that good performers consume advice and feedback from nearly everywhere, yet hold back from asking their leader for guidance. The author diagnoses the cause as ego management, since team members want to prove their competence and preserve their independence in the leader's eyes. The central move is to reframe asking for advice as a sign of confidence rather than weakness and to treat the leader explicitly as a coach. Doing so, the piece argues, yields more than individual insight: it opens a continuing dialogue about what high performance looks like, with influence flowing both ways. It closes with a warning that many team members regret not having used their leader's experience while they had the chance.
points: The piece locates the blockage in the team member's desire to look competent and independent, which leads them to seek input from every source except the leader best placed to help.
Asking one's leader for candid assessment of one's skills and what to do differently is recast as an act of confidence, not an admission of weakness.
Engaging a leader as a coach creates an ongoing conversation about what high performance requires, and that mutual influence is what sustains the relationship.
The author frames the leader's savvy and street-smarts as a time-limited resource that team members often regret failing to use.
quotes: Good leaders are learning machines. They constantly consume information, advice, and feedback in order to improve. They seek input from a wide variety of sources and take instruction from those with more experience than they have.

Attempting to prove one’s competence and worth in the eyes of their leader inhibits many team members from seeking the bountiful wisdom contained in their leader’s experience. To maintain their independence and stake out their own path, team members often seek out and digest input from just about every source except the person that can help them the most.

Asking for advice and wisdom from your leader is a sign of confidence, not weakness. Treat your leader as a coach and inquire how they see your skills, how they would advise you to do things differently, and what insights they might offer to make you more effective.

More importantly, engaging your leader as a coach will create an ongoing dialogue about how both parties view high performance and the critical ingredients that foster it. As with all great coaching relationships, mutual influence is what keeps the conversation going.

Given the savvy, street-smarts, and experience of your leader, it would be a shame not to take full advantage of their wisdom while you can. Too many team members fail to do so. They regret it years later.
